claims.text: The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is an additive-manufactured dual-nanoprecipitation alloy.
The nanoscale precipitates have heterogeneous elemental distributions.
Integrating oxidation with APT will reveal atomic-scale oxidation mechanisms in this alloy.
Preferential elemental segregation at nanoprecipitates drives the formation of protective oxide layers.
The proposed treatment oxidizes the alloy in air at 800°C for 1 hour, rapidly quenches it, and subsequently analyzes it by APT.
Rapid quenching freezes the oxidation state for subsequent characterization.
The integrated protocol ensures in situ capture without ambient interference.
Nanoprecipitates act as sites for selective elemental oxidation and segregation.
Elevated temperature produces differential oxidation kinetics among the alloy's constituent elements.
Differential oxidation kinetics cause localized elemental redistribution.
APT can resolve three-dimensional atomic-scale compositional changes associated with oxidation.
Protective oxide layers may form at nanoprecipitate interfaces.
APT will reveal Cr- or Ti-enriched nanoscale regions at the periphery of nanoprecipitates.
Cr- or Ti-enriched regions correlate with the evolution of protective oxide layers.
The resulting protective oxide layers enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Conventional ex situ oxidation analyses of cast and wrought counterparts do not capture the real-time evolution of elemental redistribution.
The relevant oxidation-induced effects will occur primarily within the first few nanometers of nanoprecipitate boundaries.
Rapid oxidation kinetics, insufficient APT resolution, or subtle compositional changes could place the proposed effects below the detection threshold.

contradictions.description: The protocol states that oxidation is followed by rapid quenching and then APT analysis, which is a quenched-state or quasi-in-situ measurement rather than real-time observation during oxidation. This conflicts with descriptions of 'in situ capture' and capturing the 'real-time evolution' of redistribution.

The baseline is defined as ex situ analysis of cast and wrought counterparts, whereas the falsification experiment uses two sets with identical initial microstructures that differ only in integrated versus conventional ex situ processing. These are materially different control definitions.
